title: THE BIBLE SAYS A MAN MAY BE BETTER OFF LIVING ON A ROOFTOP THAN INSIDE HIS OWN HOME WITH HIS WIFE. BUT THE REAL WARNING IS DEEPER THAN MOST PEOPLE REALIZE.
paragraphs: THE BIBLE SAYS A MAN MAY BE BETTER OFF LIVING ON A ROOFTOP THAN INSIDE HIS OWN HOME WITH HIS WIFE. BUT THE REAL WARNING IS DEEPER THAN MOST PEOPLE REALIZE.

Proverbs 21:9 contains one of Scripture’s most uncomfortable pictures of marriage. It exposes how a home can become emotionally unbearable, why constant conflict destroys intimacy, and how Jesus Christ can restore what pride, bitterness, and unhealed wounds have torn apart.
Imagine a man sitting alone on the corner of his roof.
The sun is disappearing. The evening air is cold. His back is pressed against a wall, and beneath him is everything he once prayed for.
His wife is inside.
His children may be sleeping.
The furniture is there. The food is there. The bed is there.
Everything that should make a house feel like home is waiting just a few feet away.
But he doesn't want to go inside.
Not because he doesn't love his family.
Not necessarily because he wants another woman.
Not because he has forgotten his responsibilities.
But because somewhere along the way, the place where he was supposed to find companionship became the place where he expected another argument.
Another accusation.
Another exhausting conversation where nobody feels heard.
Another night when one wrong word could start a war.
And sitting outside, exposed to the elements, somehow feels easier than walking through his own front door.
Now imagine something equally heartbreaking.
Inside that house is a wife who also feels alone.
She remembers when her husband used to listen.
She remembers when he looked at her with tenderness instead of irritation.
She remembers the promises, the laughter, the prayers, and the dreams they once shared.
But now she feels invisible.
And the more invisible she feels, the louder she becomes.
The louder she becomes, the farther he withdraws.
The farther he withdraws, the more desperately she tries to be heard.
Until two people who once promised to love each other are living in the same house while slowly becoming strangers.
One escapes through silence.
The other fights through words.
And neither realizes how deeply the marriage is bleeding.
Then Scripture gives us a picture so uncomfortable that we cannot simply read past it.
“It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.” — Proverbs 21:9, KJV
Read that again.
Not because God is mocking women.
Not because Scripture gives husbands permission to abandon their wives.
And certainly not because every woman who raises a concern, expresses pain, or confronts wrongdoing is quarrelsome.
The verse is exposing something far more serious.
A beautiful house can become a miserable place when destructive conflict is allowed to rule inside it.
And before anyone uses this proverb as a weapon against their spouse, we need to understand what God actually said.
Because the Hebrew text reveals something that many modern readers miss.
The original Hebrew reads:
טוֹב לָשֶׁבֶת עַל־פִּנַּת־גָּג מֵאֵשֶׁת מִדְיָנִים וּבֵית חָבֶר
Ṭov lashevet ʿal-pinnat-gag, meʾeshet midyanim uveit chaver.
A close translation is:
“Better to live on a corner of a roof than with a woman of quarrels and a shared house.”
Notice the expression אֵשֶׁת מִדְיָנִים (ʾeshet midyanim).
It describes a woman characterized by quarrels or contentious disputes.
The Hebrew word midyanim concerns strife and contention. The proverb is not describing a wife who respectfully disagrees, asks difficult questions, or refuses to tolerate injustice.
It portrays a pattern of destructive conflict.
And the contrast is deliberately shocking.

In ancient Israel, houses commonly had flat rooftops that could serve as usable outdoor spaces. A rooftop corner, however, offered little of the comfort and protection associated with the rooms below.
The proverb imagines someone preferring that exposed, restricted place over the discomfort of living amid continual contention.
It is wisdom expressed through vivid comparison, not a command to move onto a roof.
The point is not that a rooftop is a healthy solution to marital problems.
The point is that peace is so valuable that even material comfort cannot compensate for its absence.
And here is where this passage becomes dangerous if we read it without humility.
A husband can quote Proverbs 21:9 while ignoring Ephesians 5:25.
A wife can feel condemned by Proverbs 21:9 while her husband's cruelty remains unaddressed.
Both can become so determined to prove who is wrong that they forget the God who calls both of them to repentance.
Because the same Bible that warns against a contentious wife also commands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Not love her only when she is pleasant.
Not love her only when she agrees.
Not love her only when she makes life easy.
Love her with the sacrificial seriousness of Christ's example.
And Colossians 3:19 adds:
“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.” — KJV
The Greek expression behind “be not bitter” is μὴ πικραίνεσθε (mē pikrainesthe).
It forbids becoming embittered toward one's wife, carrying the sense of bitterness or harsh resentment.
A husband who continually humiliates, intimidates, belittles, or mistreats his wife cannot justify himself by pointing to her angry reactions.
Her response may need correction.
But so may the behavior that has wounded her.
And neither person's wrongdoing makes the other's wrongdoing righteous.
God does not ask us to select whichever verse condemns our spouse while ignoring the passages that confront us.
He calls us to stand beneath the authority of His entire Word.
This is where the rooftop begins to look different.
Because sometimes the man sitting there is exhausted by constant criticism.
Sometimes the woman inside is exhausted by constant neglect.
Sometimes both are contributing to the destruction.
And sometimes one spouse is genuinely suffering under the other's abusive behavior.
Those situations must not be treated as identical.

Scripture calls believers to patience, gentleness, truthfulness, and forgiveness. It does not require someone to remain exposed to violence or coercive abuse in the name of preserving an appearance of marital peace.
Safety, appropriate protection, and wise intervention matter.
But for couples caught in ordinary patterns of resentment, defensiveness, and repeated arguments, this proverb asks a painful question.
When did winning the argument become more important than protecting the relationship?
Perhaps it started with something small.
A forgotten anniversary.
A financial decision made without discussion.
A promise that was broken.
A conversation that ended in sarcasm.
A disappointment nobody properly addressed.
Then another.
And another.
Until the unresolved pain became a language of its own.
She stopped saying, “I miss you.”
Instead, she said, “You never care about me.”
He stopped saying, “I feel like I can never get anything right.”
Instead, he said, “Here we go again.”
She heard rejection.
He heard condemnation.
And every conversation became a courtroom.
Evidence was collected.
Past mistakes were presented.
Defenses were prepared.
Verdicts were announced.
But tenderness disappeared.
And the tragedy is that both people may still desperately want to be loved.
They just no longer know how to reach each other without causing another wound.
Proverbs 21:9 is not telling us that women should never speak.
It is warning us about the destructive power of habitual contention.
And that warning is relevant to every believer, regardless of sex.
Proverbs 17:1 declares:
“Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife.” — KJV
There it is again.
A small meal with peace is better than abundance surrounded by conflict.
Not because poverty is holy.
Not because silence is always peace.
But because wealth cannot purchase the relational safety that pride and bitterness have destroyed.
You can have expensive furniture and still dread coming home.
You can own a beautiful bed and still cry yourself to sleep.
You can post smiling anniversary pictures while privately wondering whether your marriage will survive another year.
You can sit beside someone in church while feeling thousands of miles away from them.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part is that people outside the marriage may never know.
They see the photographs.
God sees the conversations.
They see the wedding rings.
God sees the resentment.
They see the house.
God sees what is happening inside it.
But before we go further, there is another Scripture we need to confront.
James 3:9–10 says:

“Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God. Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.” — KJV
That should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to sing worship songs on Sunday and speak with cruelty on Monday.
It is possible to pray publicly and humiliate privately.
It is possible to quote Scripture beautifully while using words that slowly crush the person who trusts us most.
And no amount of religious language can make that contradiction acceptable.
A wife who repeatedly attacks her husband's dignity needs to examine her heart before God.
A husband who uses anger, threats, contempt, or cold indifference to control his wife needs to do the same.
A Christian marriage cannot be healed merely by determining who can quote the most verses.
It requires truth.
Repentance.
Humility.
And the willingness to stop treating a spouse like an enemy.
There is a reason Proverbs 15:1 says:
“A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.” — KJV
That does not mean every soft answer will immediately calm an angry person.
It means gentle speech is the wise alternative to words that intensify hostility.
And sometimes one of the most spiritually mature things you can say is:
“I was wrong.”
Not, “I'm sorry you feel that way.”
Not, “I'm sorry, but you made me angry.”
Not, “Fine, I'm always the bad person.”
Just:
“I was wrong. I hurt you. Please forgive me.”
Those words do not erase consequences.
They do not automatically rebuild trust.
But genuine repentance begins where excuses end.
And perhaps that is the moment some marriages have been waiting for.
Not another sermon directed at the other person.
Not another argument about who started it.
But one heart finally becoming humble enough to confess its own sin.
Yet we must go even deeper.
Because Proverbs 21:9 is not merely about a husband's desire for quiet.
It is about what happens when a relationship becomes dominated by contention.
And contention is often fed by something Scripture repeatedly exposes.
Pride.
Proverbs 13:10 says:
“Only by pride cometh contention: but with the well advised is wisdom.” — KJV
The proverb connects quarrelling with pride and contrasts it with the wisdom of receiving counsel.
Think about how pride behaves inside marriage.
Pride refuses to apologize first.
Pride remembers every offense but minimizes its own.
Pride demands understanding without offering it.
Pride would rather sleep angry than admit wrongdoing.
Pride turns correction into an insult.
Pride turns vulnerability into a competition.
And pride can make two people who love each other act as though surrendering their ego would be worse than losing their marriage.
But the Gospel confronts pride at its roots.
Because at the center of Christianity is not a Savior who demanded that sinful people make themselves worthy before He would show them mercy.
At the center is Jesus Christ.
The One who humbled Himself.
The One who served.
The One who bore the cross.
The One who did not come to excuse sin, but to save sinners.
Philippians 2:5 says:
“Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
And Philippians 2:8 describes Christ as humbling Himself and becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
That changes the conversation.
Because the Christian question is no longer simply:
“How do I get my spouse to change?”
It becomes:
“Lord, where am I refusing to become more like Jesus?”
That question is frightening.
Because it removes our favorite hiding place.
Blame.
It does not make us responsible for someone else's sins.
But it does make us accountable for our own.
And that accountability is where genuine transformation can begin.
Now consider another uncomfortable truth.
Not every quiet marriage is a peaceful marriage.
Some homes have no shouting because one spouse is afraid to speak.
Some couples rarely argue because they have emotionally given up.
Some wives have learned to swallow every concern.
Some husbands have learned to disappear into work, entertainment, or endless scrolling.
The house is quiet.
But the marriage is starving.
Biblical peace is not simply the absence of noise.
It involves righteousness, truth, love, and reconciliation.
The Greek word εἰρήνη (eirēnē), commonly translated “peace” in the New Testament, can describe peace and harmony, including the reconciled relationship with God that comes through Christ.
Romans 5:1 declares:
“Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” — KJV
That is where the deepest restoration begins.
Not with better furniture.
Not with a bigger salary.
Not even with a perfectly behaved spouse.
But with sinners being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest problem in the human heart is not simply poor communication.
It is sin.
And sin cannot be cured by communication techniques alone.
We need forgiveness.
We need a new heart.
We need the transforming grace of God.
We need the Holy Spirit to produce what our flesh cannot manufacture.
Galatians 5:22–23 identifies the fruit of the Spirit, including love, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, and temperance.
Imagine what happens when those qualities begin shaping a marriage.
Not perfection.
Not the disappearance of every disagreement.
But a different way of responding.
A husband learns to listen without immediately defending himself.
A wife learns to express pain without attacking character.
One spouse asks a question instead of making an accusation.
The other responds honestly instead of withdrawing in contempt.
They learn that disagreement does not have to become disrespect.
They learn that correction does not have to become humiliation.
They learn that forgiveness is not pretending something never happened.
And they learn that reconciliation requires more than emotional promises. It requires repentance demonstrated through changed behavior.
For some couples, that journey will require trusted pastoral guidance, professional counseling, accountability, and time.
For others, the damage may be so serious that rebuilding trust will be a long and uncertain process.
God's grace is sufficient to forgive every repentant sinner who comes to Christ.
But no human being can guarantee that every marriage will be restored, or that every relationship will become safe simply because one person decides to forgive.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical.
Forgiveness does not require denying harm.
Reconciliation requires truth and trustworthy change.
And the Bible never gives a spouse permission to demand instant trust while continuing the behavior that destroyed it.
This matters because too many wounded believers have been told to endure destructive behavior while the person harming them is never seriously confronted.
That is not a faithful application of Proverbs 21:9.
The wisdom of God must never be turned into a shield for cruelty.
Now return to that rooftop.
Imagine the husband sitting there again.
But this time, instead of rehearsing everything his wife has done wrong, he begins to pray.
“Lord, I am tired.
I am angry.
I don't know how to fix this.
But show me the truth about my own heart.
Show me where I have been selfish.
Show me where I have failed to love.
And give me the courage to face what I have been avoiding.”
Now imagine the wife inside.
She has spent the evening replaying the argument.
She has a hundred things she wants to say.
But for the first time, she stops trying to prepare the perfect response.
And she prays.
“Jesus, You know how deeply I have been hurt.
You know what I have been carrying.
Please help me speak truth without cruelty.
Help me recognize my own sins without excusing anyone else's.
And teach me how to walk in wisdom.”
Those prayers do not magically resolve the conflict.
But something important has happened.
Two people have stopped treating themselves as completely innocent.
They have brought their hearts before the One who knows them fully.
And that is where the Gospel enters the house.
Not as a decorative Bible on the coffee table.
Not as a verse posted on the wall.
But as the living truth that confronts sin and offers grace.
Perhaps you are reading this as a husband who has spent years feeling criticized.
Perhaps you are a wife who has spent years feeling unheard.
Perhaps you are single, but you grew up in a home where every evening felt like a battlefield.
Perhaps your parents never divorced, but you still carry the sound of their arguments in your memory.
Perhaps you promised yourself that your future marriage would be different.
And now, painfully, you recognize some of the same patterns emerging in your own life.
Listen carefully.
Your history may explain some of your reactions.
But it does not have to become your destiny.
In Christ, inherited patterns of sin can be confronted.
Learned habits can be challenged.
Repentance can become real.
And by God's grace, a different way of living is possible.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — KJV
That verse is not a promise that every emotional wound disappears overnight.
It is the announcement of a new reality for those who belong to Christ.
A new identity.
A new relationship with God.
A new direction for life.
The angry person does not have to defend anger as personality.
The bitter person does not have to cherish resentment as protection.
The proud person does not have to keep calling stubbornness strength.
And the wounded person does not have to pretend that healing means accepting further harm.
Jesus Christ calls us out of darkness and into truth.
That truth can be painful.
But it is also where freedom begins.
There is something else about Proverbs 21:9 that deserves our attention.
The verse appears again in closely related language in Proverbs 25:24.
Scripture repeats the rooftop comparison.
And Proverbs 21:19 adds another vivid warning:
“It is better to dwell in the wilderness, than with a contentious and an angry woman.” — KJV
These are serious warnings about destructive patterns of conflict.
Yet the same book also celebrates the value of a wise and godly wife.
Proverbs 18:22 says:
“Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD.” — KJV
And Proverbs 31:26 describes the virtuous woman:
“She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.” — KJV
Do you see the balance?
Scripture does not portray womanhood as the problem.
It contrasts destructive conduct with godly wisdom.
A wife's words can wound.
Her words can also heal.
A husband's actions can damage trust.
His actions can also demonstrate sacrificial love.
Neither husband nor wife is called to dominate the other through fear.
Both are accountable before Christ.
And both need grace.
Ephesians 4:31–32 gives a command that belongs in every Christian home:

“Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.” — KJV
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say bitterness is acceptable because your spouse disappointed you.
It does not say cruelty becomes righteous when you feel misunderstood.
It does not say a believer is exempt from repentance because the other person sinned first.
Instead, it points us back to the forgiveness we have received through Christ.
And that is the part of this message that should bring every Christian to their knees.
Because before we were ever husbands or wives, we were sinners in need of a Savior.
Before we demanded patience, we needed God's patience.
Before we demanded mercy, we needed His mercy.
Before we asked someone to forgive our failures, we needed the forgiveness purchased through the blood of Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely teach us how to behave more politely.
He gave Himself as the sacrifice for sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not minimize our guilt.
It reveals the astonishing grace of God toward those who repent and believe.
And when that Gospel truly takes root in a person's heart, it begins changing the way they treat other people.
Especially the people closest to them.
Especially the people who have seen their worst moments.
Especially the people who can no longer be impressed by their public image.
Because spiritual maturity is not measured only by how passionately you worship in a crowded church.
It is also revealed by how you speak when nobody is applauding.
How you respond when you are corrected.
How you treat someone who disagrees with you.
How you handle disappointment.
How you apologize.
How you keep your promises.
How you respond when the person you love is struggling.
And how willing you are to repent when the Holy Spirit exposes what you would rather hide.
Maybe you have spent years asking God to change your spouse.
And perhaps your spouse genuinely needs to change.
But tonight, there may be a different prayer God is calling you to pray.
“Lord, begin with me.”
Not because everything is your fault.
Not because you must carry responsibility for someone else's choices.
But because obedience to Jesus cannot be postponed until another person obeys Him first.
You cannot repent for your spouse.
You cannot force another person to become gentle.
You cannot manufacture love in a heart that refuses to change.
But you can surrender your own heart to Christ.
You can stop excusing your cruelty.
You can seek help.
You can establish necessary boundaries.
You can pursue peace without surrendering truth.
And you can trust God with the outcome.
Romans 12:18 says:
“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.” — KJV
Those opening words matter.
“If it be possible.”
Scripture recognizes that peace does not depend on one person alone.
You are responsible for your faithfulness.
You are not sovereign over someone else's response.
And for the person who has been desperately trying to save a marriage through endless self-blame, that distinction matters.
Now, I want you to think about something.
What if the greatest tragedy in that rooftop scene is not that a man is sitting outside?
What if it is that two people who once dreamed of building a home together have forgotten what a home was supposed to be?
Not a battlefield.
Not a courtroom.
Not a place where one person wins and the other loses.
But a place where truth can be spoken with love.
Where repentance is possible.
Where children can witness humility rather than constant hostility.
Where forgiveness is practiced without covering up wrongdoing.
Where Christ is honored not only through prayers but through daily conduct.
A place where people do not have to be perfect to be treated with dignity.
That is worth fighting for.
Not by fighting each other.
But by resisting the pride, sin, bitterness, and destructive habits that have been tearing the relationship apart.
And if your marriage has already suffered terrible damage, do not mistake this message for a promise of an effortless ending.
Some wounds require time.
Some relationships require outside intervention.
Some situations require separation for safety.
Some people refuse to repent.
But even when the outcome of a marriage is uncertain, the invitation of Jesus Christ remains.
Come to Him.
Bring your guilt.
Bring your grief.
Bring the sins you committed.
Bring the wounds you suffered.
Bring the truth you have been afraid to face.
Christ does not need you to manufacture a beautiful testimony before you approach Him.
He calls sinners to repentance and offers mercy through His finished work.
And no human scandal is greater than His power to redeem a repentant life.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always been bigger than a dramatic story or an emotional moment.
From scandal to grace is not the denial of what happened. It is the declaration that sin and shame do not have to have the final word when Jesus Christ brings redemption.
The cross tells us that sin is serious.
The empty tomb tells us that death has been defeated.
And the Gospel tells us that forgiveness and new life are found in Jesus Christ.
Maybe your marriage needs that truth today.
Maybe your family needs it.
Maybe the person you have become needs to be confronted by it.
And maybe someone reading these words has been pretending for years that everything is fine.
You don't have to pretend here.
If this message exposed something you need to surrender to Jesus, I want to invite you to respond with sincerity.
If you are exhausted and need prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to reveal private details or expose your spouse publicly. Sometimes the most meaningful confession begins with a few honest words spoken before God.
Someone who has almost lost hope may need to be reminded that the Lord is still at work.
But please don't allow this message to end with your own reflection.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a husband who feels defeated.
Somewhere is a wife who cries when nobody is watching.
Somewhere is a young couple learning the wrong way to handle conflict.
Somewhere is a single person who needs to understand biblical marriage before entering it.
And somewhere is a person who has been using Scripture to condemn others while refusing to examine their own heart.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to send a passive-aggressive message to your spouse.
But because God's Word deserves to reach beyond the people who already know it.
I also want to speak personally to those who believe this kind of ministry matters.
Every article we write, every biblical resource we share, and every person we hope to reach represents a continuing opportunity to proclaim Christ.
But sustaining and expanding that work requires people who are willing to stand alongside the mission.
Not merely to receive more content.
But to participate in helping this ministry continue producing and sharing Christ-centered teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources.
We honor that distinction because biblical truth matters more than any fundraising appeal.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
It is the opportunity to stand with a mission that seeks to make Jesus Christ known.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, your prayers, comments, and shares matter.
You can help introduce this ministry to someone who may never have encountered it otherwise.
These resources are part of our desire to help people move beyond a passing emotional response and toward lasting biblical understanding, spiritual maturity, and a life shaped by the Gospel.
Your prayers are treasured.
And your willingness to share biblical truth can help carry the message to someone who desperately needs to hear it.
But before you leave, I want to bring you back to the man on the rooftop.
The sun has disappeared.
The house is quiet.
He is still sitting there.
Perhaps he is thinking about the day he first met his wife.
Perhaps he remembers the promises they made before God.
Perhaps he is wondering how two people who once loved each other so deeply became so skilled at hurting each other.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, he is no longer asking only what is wrong with her.
He is asking what needs to change in him.
Downstairs, perhaps his wife is asking the same question.
We do not know what happens next.
Proverbs does not tell us whether that man comes down from the roof.
It does not tell us whether the marriage survives.
It does not promise that every wounded relationship will be restored.
But the Gospel gives us a greater hope than a perfectly written ending.
It gives us a living Savior.
A Savior who forgives repentant sinners.
A Savior who confronts pride.
A Savior who teaches us to love.
A Savior who can transform hearts that have spent years resisting Him.
And whether your marriage is thriving, struggling, broken, or beyond your power to repair, Jesus Christ remains worthy of your trust and obedience.
So do not leave this passage merely asking whether your spouse has become quarrelsome.
Ask whether your own heart has become hardened.
Ask whether your words are building up or tearing down.
Ask whether you have confused control with love.
Ask whether you have been demanding grace while refusing to extend it.
And above all, ask whether Jesus Christ truly reigns over the way you live when nobody else is watching.
Because a house does not become a godly home simply because a Bible sits inside it.
A home is shaped by the people who live there, the truth they obey, the sins they confront, and the grace they practice.
And sometimes the first sign that God is rebuilding something is not a dramatic miracle.
It is a softened heart.
An honest confession.
A sincere apology.
A necessary boundary.
A willingness to seek help.
A prayer whispered through tears.
Or one person finally choosing obedience to Christ over the need to win.
The saddest thing about the man on the rooftop was never how far he had climbed above his house, but how far peace had disappeared from the hearts beneath it.
